title: Declare variables of different types
description:
Write a function `build_profile(first_name, last_name, country, city, age, year, is_married)` that returns a dict with keys `first_name`, `last_name`, `full_name` (first + last, space-separated), `country`, `city`, `age`, `year`, and `is_married`.

Covers source items 3-12: declaring a first_name, last_name, full_name, country, city, age, year, and is_married variable are each their own numbered item in the source, but none has a fixed value to check - what's actually being tested is declaring variables of the right types (str, int, bool) and combining two of them (full_name), which this single function does for all of them at once.
hints: Idea to consider: build the dict directly from the parameters, plus one computed value
full_name isn't one of the parameters - it's built from two of them with an f-string or string concatenation, the same as any other derived value.
Return a dict literal with the seven parameters as keys, plus 'full_name' computed as f'{first_name} {last_name}'.
expected_behavior: Returns a dict with all eight keys, full_name derived from first_name and last_name.
solution:
def build_profile(first_name, last_name, country, city, age, year, is_married):
    return {
        "first_name": first_name,
        "last_name": last_name,
        "full_name": f"{first_name} {last_name}",
        "country": country,
        "city": city,
        "age": age,
        "year": year,
        "is_married": is_married,
    }
explanation: A dict literal declares several named values at once, the same idea as ten separate variable declarations - full_name shows that a variable doesn't have to come from a parameter directly, it can be computed from others.
